newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia Dec palmoil exports seen up, output off.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia Dec palmoil exports seen up, output off.

text.p: Indonesian palm oil exports totalled an estimated 180,000 tonnes in December, compared with 170,000 tonnes in November, traders told Reuters on Friday.
They said crude palm oil production was an estimated 380,000 tonnes in December, down from 390,000 tonnes in November.
Indonesia's crude palm oil production declined in the last quarter of 1996 because of bad weather and the carry-over effects of a dry spell the previous year.
Traders also blamed the poor output on a fertiliser shortage, which seemed to have affected state plantations.
State plantations were forecast to produce 1.8 million tonnes of crude palm oil in 1996, and account for up to 40 percent of the country's total production.
A government official had said he expected production in state plantations to fall by up to 20 percent in 1996.
"Production in my plantation in north Sumatra was flat in December," one trader with a plantation house said.
"The decline has been sharper so far in January because of seasonal reasons. The drop will continue into early March.
"Crude palm oil prices are very good at the moment, but it's a pity we don't have much oil available to sell," he said.
A senior trader said output from his plantation in Sumatra was down by about four to five percent in December, which was an improvement over the seven percent decline in November.

"Last year there was no peak season and most plantations saw a decline in production," he said. "I do not know how my plantations are doing in January, but I don't think the decline in production will be as bad as in December."
Traders said Indonesian crude palm oil production was expected to reach 4.6 to 4.7 million tonnes in 1996, compared with 4.2 million tonnes the previous year.
The Indonesian Palm Oil Producers Association had forecast 1996 output to rise to 4.9 million tonnes due to an increase in the area under oil palm cultivation and higher yields from maturing trees.
Another trader said production fell by about three percent at his plantations in December compared with November, and added that the decline was expected to continue this month.

"There will be a seasonal decline in January, but at this stage I cannot say by how much," he said. "I'll only get the figures in early February. I don't think there'll be a big difference in January output from December."
The traders said exports in December were relatively high because of the attractive prices in Europe.
"Crude palm oil prices were better in Europe than in the local market, and this saw increased exports," one trader said. "This was despite the relatively high export tax."
He said prices in Europe were bolstered by tight freight during the year-end. "Those who had not booked vessels earlier were left scrambling for freight," he said.
